newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czechs must prepare for NATO air needs-US general.
newsitem.headline: Czechs must prepare for NATO air needs-US general.

text.p: The commander of U.S. air forces in Europe said the Czech Republic would have to make a significant contribution to air defence if it joined NATO but fighter purchases were for Prague to decide.

General Michael Ryan, chairman of Allied Air Forces Central Europe, said after talks with Czech air force chief Jiri Nekvasil that there had been no discussion of which planes the Czechs, seeking to upgrade their fleet, should buy.

"Those air forces that will be part of the alliance in future must be capable at least in the air defence mission... It was in that light that we discussed the future aircraft but we didn't get into specific types," he told a news conference.
The Czech Republic hopes to be among the first wave of post-Communist East European states to join NATO.
Czech officials have said they need about 24 fighters to replace ageing Soviet-made MiG-21s and be more compatible with NATO, but are worried by the cost.
"All the modern fighters that are out there right now, from the West, are very compatible," Ryan said, declining to recommend any plane.
"It is a question of economics, the kinds of capabilities they want and that will be a decision for the Czech Republic."
McDonnell Douglas Corp and Lockheed Martin of the United States and the Anglo-Swedish Gripen consortium of British Aerospace and SAAB have offered their supersonic planes at major discounts.

"NATO is in no position to tell the nations what kind of equipment to buy. What NATO will urge is that whatever kind of equipment is inter-operable so that we can do our missions together," Ryan said.
Czech Defence Minister Miloslav Vyborny said on Monday that no decision on which supersonic jet would be purchased was expected soon.
Some critics in the Czech Republic have questioned whether the air force is adequate for NATO tasks.
But Ryan said any decision to offer NATO membership to an applicant would depend on a number of issues -- political, economic and diplomatic.
"Not just one single issue will determine to whom invitations are issued," he said.
